messages.subject: Applying Detection Function to a Subsample of Data using MRDS
parts:
Hi,

I created a detection function based on 136 sightings using the MRDS
analysis engine (DS model: MCDS). For my analysis I need to get densities
from singular survey days. I therefore applied the above mentioned
detection function to subsamples of the survey data. This does only work
if there are at least two sightings on one transect within this subsample=
.
It does not work if there is only one sighting in the subsample. And it
also doesn=B4t work if there are several transects with one sighting each
within this subsample. Precondition for the analysis to work seems to be
that there is at least one transect with two sightings on it. It even
works if there is only one transect in the subsample =96 as long as it ha=
s
two sightings on it.

If anybody has an explanation or suggestions regarding this issue please
let me know.

Thanks

Linn

messages.author: fa57a82da3096f30
messages.subject: Re: Applying Detection Function to a Subsample of Data using MRDS
parts:
Dear Ms. Lehnert:

It sounds bad the way you describe it. I would hate to think that someone
somewhere is using such methods for estimates of nuclear weapons. I don't
think it is likely to be robust because the variance inherent in so few
measures will be enough to choke us all.

Can you find some logical categories that are ecologically valid to clump
your observations and get the variance down to where it can at least be
useful in estimating what sample size you need to feel there's firmament
beneath your feet?

It appears that you are basically practicing convenience sampling because
the organisms are so uncooperative. My suggestion is to talk with someon=
e
like Dr. Salganik (Department of Sociology, 1180 Amsterdam Avenue, New York=
,
NY 10027, USA. mjs...@columbia.edu) who has the background to make concret=
e
realistic recommendations so you are not left in the wilderness surrounded
by laughing acronyms.

See their research in J Urban
Health.<http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16937083> 2006
Nov;83(6 Suppl):i98-112.
Variance estimation, design effects, and sample size calculations for
respondent-driven sampling.

My feeling, if I understand what you are saying, is that Poisson is the way
to go for looking at these sparse data across the unhelpful transcepts.

Dwight Hines
St. Augustine, Florida
IndyMedia

messages.author: 12f269733c6eb9a2
messages.subject: Re: Applying Detection Function to a Subsample of Data using MRDS
parts:
Linn:

You data do not seem to support density estimates at the level of days.=20
Remember variability in your density estimates are composed of 2 pieces,=20
uncertainty in the detection function that allows you to estimate the=20
number of animals in the area covered by your transects, and variability=20
in the number of animals detected between transects (encounter rate). It=20
is unlikely that the variance estimates for densities estimated on a=20
daily level will be reliable, even if Distance will calculate them. Have=20
a read through section 3.6 on variance estimation in Buckland et al. (200=
1).
